Transformers

Transformer fundamentals

Turn a sequence of vectors into a sequence that uses context. Start with one attention head, then see how it fits into a model for text or images.

Companion to lessons 03–07 · Bridge to lessons 08–09
Prerequisites: Python lists, vectors, dot products, and matrix multiplication

What you will learn

After this guide, you should be able to calculate a small attention matrix, explain a causal mask, and trace the data through a Transformer block. You should also be able to explain what changes when the input is a sequence of image patches.

Start with a concrete task. A language model reads “the cat sat” and predicts the next token. At the “sat” position, attention can combine information from earlier tokens. A Vision Transformer performs a similar calculation over patch vectors from an image.

1. Represent the input

Write the input as a matrix X with one row per position. For n positions and d_model features, its shape is [n, d_model]. We omit the batch dimension here to make each calculation visible.

For text, a tokenizer produces token IDs and an embedding table maps them to vectors. For images, divide the image into patches, flatten each patch, and apply a learned linear projection. Neither kind of input arrives with useful semantic vectors for free: the embedding or projection is learned.

For example, a 32 × 32 RGB image divided into 8 × 8 patches produces 16 patches. Each flattened patch contains 192 numbers. A projection from 192 to 64 features gives a [16, 64] sequence before adding any classification token.

2. Calculate one attention head

Each position supplies a query, a key, and a value. A query is compared with every visible key; the resulting weights determine how to combine the values. The three projections are learned separately.

Q = X W_Q                 [n, d_k]
K = X W_K                 [n, d_k]
V = X W_V                 [n, d_v]

S = Q Kᵀ / √d_k           [n, n]
A = softmax(S + mask)     [n, n]   softmax along each row
O = A V                   [n, d_v]

The dot product measures compatibility between a query and a key. Dividing by √d_k helps control the scale of the scores. Softmax turns each row into nonnegative weights that sum to one. Finally, matrix multiplication with V mixes the information at different positions.

A calculation you can check by hand

Take a query q = [0, 1], two visible keys [1, 0] and [0, 1], and values [2, 0] and [0, 1]. The scaled scores are [0, 0.707]. Softmax gives approximately [0.330, 0.670], so the output is 0.330 × [2, 0] + 0.670 × [0, 1] = [0.660, 0.670].

Keep the two outputs distinct: A contains weights over positions, while O contains new feature vectors. Attention weights are not vocabulary probabilities and, by themselves, do not establish why a model made a prediction.

3. Control what each position sees

A next-token language model must not read future tokens while learning to predict them. For row i, set the score at column j to negative infinity whenever j > i. Apply this mask before softmax; those positions then receive exactly zero weight.

             key 0   key 1   key 2
query 0        ✓       —       —
query 1        ✓       ✓       —
query 2        ✓       ✓       ✓

The current token remains visible because the training target at that position is the next token. A padding mask serves a different purpose: it hides artificial padding positions. For ordinary image classification, a Vision Transformer usually allows every patch to attend to every other patch.

Check your understanding: if you change the last input vector, which earlier outputs may change? With causal attention, none of them should change. Without the causal mask, they may change.

4. Build a Transformer block

One head is only part of a Transformer. Multiple heads use separate projections to mix information in different feature spaces. Concatenate their outputs, then project the result back to d_model features so it can be added to the input.

H = X + MultiHeadAttention(LayerNorm(X))
Y = H + FeedForward(LayerNorm(H))

This is a common pre-normalization layout; the original Transformer used a different normalization order. Layer normalization rescales features within each position. Residual additions preserve a direct path through the block. The feed-forward network applies the same small nonlinear network to each position independently.

Attention exchanges information between positions; the feed-forward network transforms features within a position. Stacking these blocks builds depth. Positional information is also needed: attention alone does not know which row came first. Models can add position embeddings or encode relative position inside the attention calculation.

For a concrete shape check, let d_model = 64 and use four heads with d_k = d_v = 16. Each head outputs [n, 16]; concatenation gives [n, 64]. Doubling the sequence length makes the number of entries in each dense attention matrix four times larger.

How an induction head predicts the next token

In this example, “copying head” refers to an induction head. It helps a Transformer predict the next token by looking up what followed the same token earlier in the current text. If the model sees z m r … z, the earlier z provides a reason to predict m. If the text had instead been z k r … z, the same head could favor k with exactly the same learned weights. The weights encode the lookup rule. The current text supplies the answer.

To trace the lookup, start at m. In a simple two-layer circuit, a head in the first layer records information about the preceding z at the position of m. At the final z, the induction head in the second layer uses that information to match its query to the key at m. It reads the value there and raises the score for m as the next token. Olsson et al., In-context Learning and Induction Heads.

Takehi and colleagues turned the problem around. They gave an LLM the weights from the middle layers of three small Transformers and asked it to identify the copying heads. In Experiment 3, they report that its choices matched the heads they found by running the models on a random string repeated twice. Takehi et al., Sparks of Weight-Space Programming.

5. Use the block for language and vision

Two common uses of the same basic architecture
ChoiceNext-token language modelVision Transformer classifier
InputToken embeddingsProjected image patches
VisibilityCausal attentionTypically all patches visible
Output headVocabulary logits at each positionClass logits from a classification token or pooled features
Example objectiveCross-entropy against the next tokenCross-entropy against an image label

These are two configurations, not a rule that every text or vision model must follow. For example, visual generation uses other objectives. Separate the input representation, attention visibility, output head, and training objective when comparing architectures.

Python exercise · Calculate and test attention

Run a single attention head over three hand-chosen vectors. Then change the mask and inputs to test your predictions. This exercise computes a forward pass; it does not train a model or implement a complete Transformer.

No packages or GPU needed. Browser execution uses Pyodide, loaded only when you press Run. Each run starts fresh. Your code runs in this browser.

Open the exercise to load its code.

Your output will appear here.

Expected result

Attention weights (3 x 3):
  [1.000, 0.000, 0.000]
  [0.330, 0.670, 0.000]
  [0.248, 0.248, 0.503]
Output vectors (3 x 2):
  [2.000, 0.000]
  [0.660, 0.670]
  [1.503, 0.752]

Displayed values are rounded; the unrounded attention rows sum to one.

Make three changes

  1. Set CAUSAL = False. Predict which zero entries will disappear, then run the code.
  2. Restore the causal mask and change only the last row of X to [4.0, -2.0]. Verify that the first two output vectors remain unchanged. Repeat without the mask.
  3. Restore the original input and set every row of W_V to zero. Explain why the attention weights stay the same while every output vector becomes zero.

Take this into the project course

Submit the attention matrices with and without a causal mask, one hand-calculated output vector, and your explanation of the future-token test. These are the first evidence items for preparation exercise A.

In preparation exercise B, reuse this understanding when implementing a small Transformer block with automatic differentiation. Add a language-model head for text and a classification head for image patches. In the final multimodal agent, distinguish the model that encodes images from the controller that chooses tools.

Exit check: explain why an attention matrix can have shape [16, 16] while its output has shape [16, 64]. Then explain why changing the mask does not change either shape.

Required reading

For Lesson 6, read these selections in order.

  1. Olsson et al., In-context Learning and Induction Heads (2022). Read “Induction Heads” under “Key Concepts.” For z m r … z, identify which earlier position the final z attends to and which token that helps it predict.
  2. Elhage et al., A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (2021). Read “Induction Heads” in the section on two-layer models. In z m r … z, what does the first head write at the position of m, and how does the second head use it?
  3. Takehi et al., Sparks of Weight-Space Programming (2026). Read Experiment 3. How did the authors use a repeated random string to check which heads the LLM had identified from the weights?

Further reading

  • Attention Is All You Need — compare Figure 1 and Section 3.2 with the block and attention equations above.
  • An Image Is Worth 16×16 Words — trace how image patches become the input sequence in Figure 1.

Homework · Find copying heads from weights

Reproduce the Python-model row of Figure 1 in Takehi et al.’s Experiment 3. You will rank candidate heads from the released weights, then check your predictions against the authors’ measurements. This is individual work for preparation exercise B. Read the experiment and Figure 1.

Set up on your laptop

Use Python 3 with NumPy on a CPU. Save these three files in the same folder under the names shown. weight_space_homework.py is the course starter. The authors provide the Python-trained model weights, blocks.npz (28 MB), and the behavioral measurements, heads.json.

python -m pip install numpy
python weight_space_homework.py

Predict, then check

  1. Rank the heads from weights. Start with source head L0H5. The script ranks all six heads in layer 2 by how well their query–key weights match the information the source head writes. Record the highest-ranked head and its C_k score. Indices start at zero.
  2. Repeat for layer 3. Change SOURCE_LAYER, SOURCE_HEAD, and TARGET_LAYER to 2, 2, 3. Run again and record the top two heads and their scores. Keep both predictions before opening the behavioral results.
  3. Check both runs. For each setting, run python weight_space_homework.py --check. The second table shows how much attention each head paid to the earlier successor when the authors ran the full model on a repeated 40-character string. They label a head as copying when its induct score exceeds 0.20. Compare the head IDs that pass this cutoff with your predictions and the Python row in Figure 1.

Submit with exercise B. Include your code and a table with the source head, candidate head, weight score, and behavioral score. Include one lower-ranked head for comparison. State whether you recovered all three reported copying heads, describe any mismatch, and explain why the two scores can have different values for the same head. Compare your weight scores with the authors’ run record.
